average-return-calculator.assumptionNote: Assumes each return is one full period (e.g. one year), gains are reinvested, and no deposits or withdrawals happen in between.
benefits: Shows the true compounded return (geometric mean) that your money actually experienced.
The volatility drag figure quantifies exactly what ups and downs cost you.
Doubles as a fund check: compare a fund's advertised average with its real CAGR.
Runs on any return series: stocks, mutual funds, business revenue, or savings rates.

faqs.a: The arithmetic mean adds the yearly percentages and divides by the count. The geometric mean (CAGR) compounds them: it is the single constant rate that grows the start value to the end value. Money compounds geometrically, so the geometric mean is the honest one.
faqs.q: Arithmetic vs geometric mean - which is right?

faqs.a: Volatility drag = arithmetic mean minus geometric mean. Swings cost you: +50% then -50% averages to 0% arithmetically but leaves you at 75% of your money (a 25% loss). The bigger the swings, the bigger the drag.
No. The geometric mean cannot be computed if any single-period return is -100% or worse, because the investment hit zero and compounding stops. The tool flags this instead of inventing a number.
faqs.q: Can I include a year I lost everything?

faqs.a: Yes - enter each year's return as a percentage, in order. The tool treats each entry as one full compounding period, so monthly figures give a monthly average, not an annualised one.
faqs.q: Does it work for monthly returns?

faqs.a: 6.50% arithmetic, 6.31% geometric, 1,277.34 final value on 1,000 invested, and 0.19% volatility drag. The -4% year is what pulls the geometric mean below the simple average.
Roughly: annualised return = (end / start)^(1 / years) - 1. That is the geometric mean of the yearly returns, so this calculator gives the same answer when you enter each year's percentage.
faqs.q: How do I annualise a multi-year total return?

average-return-calculator.formula:
Arithmetic mean = (r1 + r2 + ... + rn) / n
Geometric mean (CAGR) = ((1 + r1) x (1 + r2) x ... x (1 + rn))^(1/n) - 1
Volatility drag = arithmetic mean - geometric mean
(returns r entered as percentages, e.g. 8 for 8%)
howTo: Enter each period's return as a percentage (8 for 8%, -4 for a 4% loss), separated by commas.
The geometric mean (CAGR) is the headline: your true compounded yearly return.
Compare it with the arithmetic mean - the gap is the volatility drag.
The final value shows what 1,000 invested would have grown to.
keyFacts: The geometric mean is always less than or equal to the arithmetic mean.
A single -100% period makes the geometric mean undefined (money hit zero).

average-return-calculator.quickAnswer: Enter yearly returns as percentages and get the true compounded average. For 8, 12, -4, 10: the arithmetic mean is 6.50%, but the geometric mean (CAGR) - the rate your money actually compounded at - is 6.31%. The 0.19 point gap is volatility drag, the cost of the ups and downs. 1,000 invested would have grown to 1,277.34. Always judge investments by the geometric mean, never the simple average.
